title: Varieties form nested groups for the same reason species do

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Varieties form nested groups for the same reason species do

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Domestic and natural varieties fall into groups subordinate to groups (sub-varieties under varieties under species) for the same reason species do, namely closeness of descent combined with various degrees of modification.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The origin of the existence of groups subordinate to groups, is the same with varieties as with species, namely, closeness of descent with various degrees of modification.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XIII, “Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs”; section “Classification of varieties”. Scope: varieties and breeds of domestic and wild species

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch13-06: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.58

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Genomics can resolve the claim in selected breeds and species. Data and labels are fragmented, so the full stated scope would require extensive compilation.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Within domestic breeds and well-sampled wild varieties, test whether recognized sub-varieties form genetically nested descent clusters and whether phenotypic distance increases along that hierarchy. Congruent genetic nesting supports descent with modification.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Variety and sub-variety labels are inconsistently defined.

Hybridization and repeated artificial selection blur nested descent.

No harmonized dataset spans domestic and natural varieties.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Where pedigrees exist, nested breed groups can be compared with descent without adopting a new definition of variety. Public genomes and breed inventories cover a few domesticated species well and leave most wild varieties out, so only a restricted scope is testable. Genomic data break the circularity of testing morphology with groups that morphology defined, at the cost of months of cross-study harmonization.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For domestic breeds and wild varieties with known pedigrees or genomic relationships, test whether morphology and named subgroups form a nested hierarchy that matches descent, with deeper splits corresponding to greater modification. The claim is confirmed if breed groups recover the pedigree better than a non-hierarchical clustering, and refuted if varieties of known close descent are morphologically scattered among distant breeds.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Breeds were often defined by the same external traits used to test nested morphological groups, which makes a purely morphological test circular.

Wild 'varieties' are delimited inconsistently, so the natural-variety half of the scope is much weaker than the breed half.

Genomic pedigrees are dense for dogs, horses, chickens and a few crops, and sparse for most domesticated and wild varieties.
